kakekotoba.interaction: Matsuho is a real place name (bay in Awaji), but its initial まつ simultaneously evokes 松 'pine' and, through the poem's opening こぬ人を, resonates with 待つ 'to wait' — the speaker waiting for a lover who does not come; the place name carries the emotional weight of waiting even though it is nominally just a toponym

やく literally describes the salt-makers' fires reducing brine (moshio) at Matsuho bay, but it is grammatically fused with the following もしほの身もこがれ image so that the 'burning' of the salt kilns and the 'burning/scorching' of the speaker's body with longing are experienced as the same act of combustion

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 焦がれ（塩が焦げる／身が焦がれる）
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 恋い焦がれる（恋情に身を焦がす）
kakekotoba.interaction: こがれ describes both the physical scorching of the seaweed/brine in the salt-making process (焦がれ) and the speaker's emotional burning with unfulfilled longing (恋い焦がれる) — the two meanings are fused into a single image via the mo-shio simile, making this the poem's central pivot

jokotoba.text: まつほの浦の夕なぎにやくやもしほの
jokotoba.function: An extended (well over 5 morae) descriptive preface describing the evening calm at Matsuho bay and the burning of salt-brine seaweed, composed specifically for this poem to lead sonically and imagistically into 身もこがれつつ — the salt slowly scorching over a low fire mirrors the speaker's heart slowly consumed by longing

honkadori.source_poem: 風をいたみ岩うつ波のおのれのみ砕けてものを思ふころかな (attributed source imagery of salt-burning at Matsuho ura is drawn from an earlier anonymous/Man'yō-era convention of 藻塩焼く imagery associated with Matsuho no ura in Awaji)
honkadori.function: Draws on the established poetic association of Matsuho no ura with salt-burning (moshio) imagery, inherited from earlier Man'yōshū-period descriptions of the Awaji coast, to lend the burning-longing metaphor an air of traditional authority

kigo.note: 夕なぎ (evening calm at the shore) is conventionally associated with summer evenings at the coast in classical poetics, when the wind dies down at dusk over calm water; here it sets the tranquil, suspended scene of waiting at dusk that frames the salt-burning image, though the poem's dominant imagery of 藻塩 (moshio) production is itself a genre convention tied to coastal life rather than a strict season

bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker waits at evening for a lover who does not come, framed through the calm evening scene at Matsuho bay where salt-makers tend their brine fires
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's own body/heart burns and is consumed with longing, just as the moshio seaweed is scorched over the salt-fires
bipartite.pivot_note: The entire kami-no-ku functions as an extended jokotoba built on the coastal salt-burning scene at Matsuho, and the shimo-no-ku reveals that this scene is not mere description but a sustained implicit simile: the slow, smoldering combustion of moshio brine over a low fire mirrors the speaker's own heart being slowly consumed by unfulfilled longing for the absent lover named in the poem's very first words (こぬ人を)

source_jp:

まつほの浦の
